newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ifo says Buba should keep interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Ifo says Buba should keep interest rates steady.

text.p: The Bundesbank should keep its interest rates unchanged as long as there are no signs of a threat to price stability, but circumstances may yet force it to move rates one way or the other, the Ifo economic research institute said on Tuesday.
Ifo said in its half-yearly economic report that monetary policy was expansionary at present, particularly if taking into account the weakness of the mark.
"If one incorporates the exchange rate constellation, monetary conditions are providing very strong impetus for the economy overall," Ifo said.

The monetary environment is partly or even wholly offsetting the demand-curbing impact of government spending cuts to consolidate the budget, so that the policy mix overall is not standing in the way of the economic recovery, Ifo said.
"As long as there are no signs of risks to price stability, monetary policy should stick to its current course, which means leaving key rates at the current low level."
Speculation is mounting that the Bundesbank may raise its main money market rate, the repo rate, from the current level of 3.00 percent to stem the mark's steep drop against the dollar this year.
But Ifo said there were circumstances that could move the Bundesbank to lower rates.

For example, if the economy failed to keep recovering, resulting in a drop in bond yields, a further rate reduction would be appropriate to maintain the margin between long-term and short-term interest rates, Ifo said.
A rate cut would also be appropriate to counteract a surge in the mark if Europe's planned monetary union were delayed, Ifo said.
But the Bundesbank may also have to raise interest rates if expectations of a weak Euro become so dominant that the mark comes under increased pressure to depreciate, Ifo said.
In that case, "the Bundesbank may see itself compelled to raise key rates because of the threat of a loss of confidence and because of inflation risks."
The institute urged governments to pursue credible budget consolidation strategies as this would allay fears of a soft euro, renewed market turbulence and a mark appreciation.
